name: pair-for-each
summary: Applies a procedure to each successive PAIR of a list for effect, saving each cdr first so the procedure may splice the list it is walking.
explanation: pair-for-each is for-each moved one level down: instead of the element it hands over the pair, so (car p) is the element and (cdr p) is everything still ahead. There is no accumulator -- the result is unspecified and must not be used -- so whatever this walk produces goes into a variable you close over, or into the list itself. That second option is the point. pair-for-each saves each pair's cdr BEFORE calling proc, which means proc may call set-cdr! on the pair it was handed and the walk still reaches the end. That makes in-place deletion, compaction, and splicing writable as a walk rather than a hand-rolled cursor loop. The standard idiom puts a throwaway anchor pair in front of the list so the first real node can be removed like any other. The one thing to keep in mind is that the walk follows the cdrs it saved, not the list as it now stands: nodes you unlinked are still visited, and side effects recorded inside proc can therefore fire on structure that is already gone.

examples.note: (1 2 3) (2 3) (3) -- each step sees a whole tail, not an element.

examples.code:
(define readings '(3 7 6 10))
(define gaps '())
(pair-for-each (lambda (p)
                 (if (pair? (cdr p)) (set! gaps (cons (- (cadr p) (car p)) gaps))))
               readings)
(display (list 'readings readings 'gaps (reverse gaps)))
(newline)
examples.note: (readings (3 7 6 10) gaps (4 -1 4)) -- with no accumulator, the answer accumulates in a closed-over variable.

examples.code:
(define live (list 1 2 3 4 5 6))
(define anchor (cons 'anchor live))
(pair-for-each (lambda (p)
                 (let drop ()
                   (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (even? (cadr p)))
                       (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop)))))
               anchor)
(display (list 'odds (cdr anchor)))
(newline)
examples.note: (odds (1 3 5)) -- the list is filtered in place during the walk, which is only safe because each cdr was saved first.

caveats: Its return value is UNSPECIFIED. Never use it. Put results in a closed-over variable or in the list itself.
proc receives a PAIR. Use (car p) for the element and (cdr p) for the rest.
The last call receives the final one-element tail, whose cdr is (). Guard with (pair? (cdr p)) before looking ahead.
proc may safely set-cdr! the pair it was handed -- the cdr was saved before the call. That is why this verb exists.

The walk follows saved cdrs, so it keeps visiting nodes you have already unlinked. A predicate matching consecutive elements must drop them in a loop, and any counter incremented inside proc will over-count.
Put a throwaway anchor pair in front of the list before splicing, or the first node cannot be removed.
After splicing, a variable still pointing at the old first node sees a stale, shorter list. Read the new head from the anchor.
It is n-ary and stops at the shortest list.
It requires proper lists. A dotted list raises rather than stopping at the improper tail.
usecases: Deleting, compacting, or splicing a list in place while walking it.
Side-effecting work that needs to compare each element with the ones after it.
Auditing a list's own node structure, since the pairs handed over are the list's nodes.

learn.concept: A walk that saves its next step before calling out can survive having the ground rewritten underneath it -- and that is exactly what in-place list surgery needs.
learn.progression: Use for-each until you need to delete from the list you are walking, and watch a hand-written loop lose its place. Then use pair-for-each with an anchor and see the deletion work. Then count the nodes it visits, compare that to the nodes that survived, and understand that the walk is following cdrs it captured rather than the list as it stands.

provenance: SRFI-1 (fold, unfold and map: pair-for-each); record authored 2026-08-04

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (flush! anchor sent?)
  (let ((seen 0))
    (pair-for-each
      (lambda (p)
        (set! seen (+ seen 1))
        (let drop ()
          (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (sent? (cadr p)))
              (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop)))))
      anchor)
    (list 'left (cdr anchor) 'nodes-walked seen)))
(define (delivered? m) (eq? (cadr m) 'sent))
(define q1 (cons 'a (list (list 'm1 'sent) (list 'm2 'queued) (list 'm3 'sent))))
(define q2 (cons 'a (list (list 'm4 'sent) (list 'm5 'sent))))
(define q3 (cons 'a (list (list 'm6 'queued))))
(display (list 'mixed (flush! q1 delivered?)
               'all (flush! q2 delivered?)
               'none (flush! q3 delivered?)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (descents xs)
  (let ((out '()) (i 0))
    (pair-for-each
      (lambda (p)
        (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (> (car p) (cadr p)))
            (set! out (cons (list i (car p) (cadr p)) out)))
        (set! i (+ i 1)))
      xs)
    (reverse out)))
(display (list 'monotone (descents '(1 2 3 4))
               'sawtooth (descents '(3 1 4 1 5))
               'falling (descents '(9 5 2))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define (walk-census xs)
  (let ((acc '()))
    (pair-for-each (lambda (p) (set! acc (cons p acc))) xs)
    (let ((ts (reverse acc)))
      (list 'nodes (length ts)
            'lengths (map length ts)
            'own-nodes (let loop ((t ts) (i 0))
                         (cond ((null? t) #t)
                               ((eq? (car t) (list-tail xs i)) (loop (cdr t) (+ i 1)))
                               (else #f)))))))
(display (list 'three (walk-census '(a b c))
               'one (walk-census '(z))
               'none (walk-census '())))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: An outbox holds messages and the delivered ones must be removed from the live list that other parts of the program are already holding. Candidates: pair-for-each with an anchor (one walk, splices in place, and every existing reference to the outbox stays valid), filter (clean and pure and the obvious answer -- it returns a NEW list, so every other holder of the old one keeps seeing delivered messages forever), delete! (the right verb if removal by value is the whole job; here the walk also has to count and could grow other duties), a hand-written cursor loop tracking the previous node (exactly what this verb is, written out, with the previous-node bookkeeping that gets the first element wrong), rebuilding the list and assigning it back to one variable (fixes that one variable and nothing else). pair-for-each is the pick because the requirement is to edit a shared structure, not to compute a new one.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: an outbox flushed in place, over a queue that keeps one message, a queue that empties completely, and a queue where nothing is delivered; each call reports what is left and how many nodes it walked. math: every descent in a sequence, reported as position and the two values, over a monotone list, a sawtooth, and a strictly falling list. cs: the pairs the walk was handed, reported as a count, their lengths, and whether each is the input's own node at that index.
row-2-audit.meta: nodes-walked is not the surviving length and is not meant to be. In the all-delivered case the walk visits three nodes and none survive, because it follows the cdrs it saved rather than the list as it stands. A count of REMOVALS incremented inside proc would be wrong for the same reason -- it fires again on nodes that were already unlinked -- which is why this report counts visits and shows the survivors rather than adding them up.
row-2-audit.eng: Editing in place is what keeps every other holder of a list correct. Rebuilding fixes the variable you assigned and quietly leaves every other reference looking at the old contents.
row-2-audit.math: A descent is an adjacent pair out of order, and the count of them is one measure of how unsorted a sequence is. Reporting the position as well as the values is what makes it actionable rather than a statistic.
row-2-audit.cs: The pairs handed over are the list's own nodes. If they were copies, set-cdr! through them would edit garbage, and every destructive use of this verb would silently do nothing.

row-3-dimension.setup: Walking a list's tails for effect rather than its elements.

rungs.code:

(pair-for-each (lambda (p) (set! logacc (cons (list (car p) (length p)) logacc))) '(1 2 3 4))
(display (reverse logacc))

rungs.domain: a stock shelf whose expired lots are unlinked in place as the shelf is walked
rungs.code:
(define lots (list (list 'a 2024) (list 'b 2027) (list 'c 2023) (list 'd 2030)))
(define shelf (cons 'shelf lots))
(define discarded '())
(pair-for-each
  (lambda (p)
    (let drop ()
      (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (< (cadr (cadr p)) 2026))
          (begin (set! discarded (cons (car (cadr p)) discarded))
                 (set-cdr! p (cddr p))
                 (drop)))))
  shelf)
(display (list 'kept (cdr shelf) 'discarded (reverse discarded)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: an event log deduplicated in place, then audited for how much of what the walk touched no longer exists
rungs.code:
(define events (list 'boot 'boot 'load 'load 'load 'run 'halt 'halt))
(define original-length (length events))
(define hd (cons 'head events))
(define seen '())
(pair-for-each
  (lambda (p)
    (set! seen (cons p seen))
    (let drop ()
      (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (eq? (car p) (cadr p)))
          (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop)))))
  hd)
(define (reachable? node)
  (let loop ((q hd))
    (cond ((not (pair? q)) #f) ((eq? q node) #t) (else (loop (cdr q))))))
(display (list 'deduped (cdr hd) 'before original-length 'after (length (cdr hd))
               'nodes-visited (length seen)
               'ghosts (count (lambda (n) (not (reachable? n))) seen)
               'stale-variable (length events)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers the walk only reads: each tail's head and length go into a variable, and the list is untouched. On the stock shelf the walk WRITES, unlinking expired lots as it passes them and recording what it threw away; the shelf changes shape underneath the walk and the walk keeps going. In the event log the walk does the same in-place edit and then the program turns around and audits itself: it counts how many nodes it was handed, how many survived, and how many of the nodes it touched are no longer reachable from the head at all. Same walk; what climbs is read-only, then write, then write-and-account-for-the-damage.
row-3-dimension.meta: The third rung prints two numbers that look wrong and are not. nodes-visited is 9 for an eight-element list because the anchor is a node too, and ghosts is 4 because the walk kept visiting nodes it had already unlinked. stale-variable is the sharpest of the three: the variable events still names the first node, whose cdr chain was edited, so it now reports 4 for a list that had 8 elements. The live head is behind the anchor, and that is the only place to read it from.
row-3-dimension.eng: Expiry sweeps run against live inventory that other code is already holding. Unlinking keeps those references correct; rebuilding the shelf would leave every one of them looking at expired stock.
row-3-dimension.math: Removing adjacent duplicates from a sorted sequence is a run-length collapse, and one pass suffices exactly because equal elements are adjacent. On an unsorted list the same walk removes only some of the duplicates, which is a specification difference and not a bug.
row-3-dimension.cs: A traversal that captures its next step is robust to mutation of the current node and blind to mutation of the rest. Counting ghosts is how that blindness gets measured instead of assumed.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (visits-tails-in-order? xs)
  (let ((acc '()))
    (pair-for-each (lambda (p) (set! acc (cons p acc))) xs)
    (let ((ts (reverse acc)))
      (and (= (length ts) (length xs))
           (let loop ((t ts) (i 0))
             (cond ((null? t) #t)
                   ((eq? (car t) (list-tail xs i)) (loop (cdr t) (+ i 1)))
                   (else #f)))))))
(display (map visits-tails-in-order? '(() (a) (a b) (1 2 3 4 5) ((x) (y)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (matches-for-each? xs)
  (let ((a '()) (b '()) (c '()))
    (pair-for-each (lambda (p) (set! a (cons (car p) a))) xs)
    (for-each (lambda (v) (set! b (cons v b))) xs)
    (pair-for-each (lambda (p) (set! c (cons p c))) xs)
    (and (equal? a b)
         (equal? (reverse a) xs)
         (let loop ((u c) (v (pair-fold cons '() xs)))
           (cond ((null? u) (null? v))
                 ((null? v) #f)
                 ((eq? (car u) (car v)) (loop (cdr u) (cdr v)))
                 (else #f))))))
(display (map matches-for-each? '(() (1) (1 2 3) (a b) ((1 2) (3)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (splice-matches-filter? xs pred)
  (let* ((pure (filter (lambda (v) (not (pred v))) xs))
         (head (cons 'h (list-copy xs))))
    (pair-for-each (lambda (p)
                     (let drop ()
                       (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (pred (cadr p)))
                           (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop)))))
                   head)
    (equal? (cdr head) pure)))
(display (map (lambda (xs) (splice-matches-filter? xs even?))
              '((1 2 3 4) (2 2 2) (1 3 5) () (2) (2 1 2 2 3))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: pair-for-each calls its procedure exactly once per element, in front-to-back order, with the list's own i-th tail; reading only (car p) it visits exactly what for-each visits, and it visits exactly the pairs pair-fold visits; and unlinking through those pairs leaves the list equal? to what a pure filter would have produced, including when the matching elements are adjacent.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all proper lists x of length n: proc is called n times, and the i-th call receives a pair eq? to list-tail(x, i); the sequence of (car p) equals the sequence for-each yields, which is x itself; the sequence of pairs equals the reverse of pair-fold(cons, (), x) node for node; and splicing out every element satisfying pred through those pairs leaves the list equal? to filter(not-pred, x)
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: identity and order of the pairs, agreement with for-each and with pair-fold, and correctness of destructive splicing. What would falsify them: a copied tail, a walk that skipped the final one-element tail, a disagreement with pair-fold about which nodes exist, or a splice that left a matching element behind. The (2 2 2) and (2 1 2 2 3) cases carry that last one -- one splice per call is NOT enough when matches are adjacent, because the walk resumes from the saved cdr and never returns to the node it just linked past.
row-4-proof.eng: Proving the pairs are the list's own nodes is what licenses set-cdr! through them. Without that, every in-place edit in this record would be editing copies and silently doing nothing.
row-4-proof.math: Restricted to (car p), pair-for-each is for-each. That containment means the wider verb needs no new mental model for the reading half of its job.
row-4-proof.cs: Comparing against a pure filter is the only check that catches the adjacent-match trap. A one-splice-per-call version passes every test whose matches are separated, which is most tests people write by hand.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (walk-with-anchor! lst f)
  (let ((head (cons 'anchor lst)))
    (pair-for-each f head)
    (cdr head)))
(define (dedupe-sorted! lst)
  (walk-with-anchor! lst
    (lambda (p)
      (let drop ()
        (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (equal? (car p) (cadr p)))
            (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop)))))))
(display (list 'runs (dedupe-sorted! (list 1 1 2 3 3 3 4))
               'none (dedupe-sorted! (list 1 2 3))
               'all (dedupe-sorted! (list 7 7 7 7))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (collect-tails lst)
  (let ((acc '()))
    (pair-for-each (lambda (p) (set! acc (cons p acc))) lst)
    (reverse acc)))
(define (pairwise-violations lst ok?)
  (let ((bad '()))
    (for-each (lambda (t i)
                (for-each (lambda (y)
                            (if (not (ok? (car t) y))
                                (set! bad (cons (list i (car t) y) bad))))
                          (cdr t)))
              (collect-tails lst) (iota (length lst)))
    (reverse bad)))
(display (list 'sorted (pairwise-violations '(1 2 3) <)
               'unsorted (pairwise-violations '(3 1 2) <)
               'dupes (pairwise-violations '(5 5) <)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (visit-all! head f)
  (let ((n 0))
    (pair-for-each (lambda (p) (set! n (+ n 1)) (f p)) head)
    n))
(define (compaction-audit lst pred)
  (let* ((head (cons 'anchor lst))
         (touched '())
         (visited (visit-all! head
                    (lambda (p)
                      (set! touched (cons p touched))
                      (let drop ()
                        (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (pred (cadr p)))
                            (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop)))))))
         (live? (lambda (node)
                  (let loop ((q head))
                    (cond ((not (pair? q)) #f)
                          ((eq? q node) #t)
                          (else (loop (cdr q))))))))
    (list 'kept (cdr head) 'visited visited 'surviving (length (cdr head))
          'ghosts (count (lambda (n) (not (live? n))) touched))))
(display (list 'some (compaction-audit (list 1 2 3 4 5 6) even?)
               'all (compaction-audit (list 2 4 6) even?)
               'none (compaction-audit (list 1 3 5) even?)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: pair-for-each hands each successive tail to a procedure for effect, having saved the cdr first.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: walk-with-anchor! is one pair-for-each wrapped in the anchor idiom, and it returns the possibly-new head; dedupe-sorted! is written on top of it as a single predicate and collapses runs of equal neighbours in place, answering correctly for a list with runs, a list with none, and a list that is one long run. math: collect-tails is one pair-for-each into a variable; pairwise-violations uses it to check every element against every later element and reports each offending triple, which is the definition of a sorted list turned into a test. cs: visit-all! is one pair-for-each that also counts; compaction-audit filters a live list through it and then reports the visited count, the surviving count, and how many of the touched nodes are no longer reachable.
row-5-emergence.meta: walk-with-anchor! is the one worth stealing: the anchor is the whole reason in-place deletion can remove the first element, and hiding it in a helper means every splicing walk written on top gets it right by construction. The cs composition then prints the number that keeps everyone honest -- visited exceeds surviving plus one whenever anything was removed, because the walk followed saved cdrs into nodes that no longer exist. Each larger function calls its helper and cannot run without it.
row-5-emergence.eng: Collapsing runs in place is what a sorted log wants after a merge. Doing it behind an anchor helper means the caller never has to think about whether the first element can be removed.
row-5-emergence.math: Checking every earlier element against every later one is the literal definition of a total order holding across a sequence. It is quadratic and it is the specification the linear adjacent-pairs check has to match.
row-5-emergence.cs: Counting ghosts turns an implementation detail into an observation. A compaction routine that reported its visit count as a length would be wrong in a way no value-level test would notice.
